Canadian writer Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature

Canadian poet Anne Carson blends poetry, prose, dialogue and translation in her literary works. Her writing draws heavily on classical Greek literature and includes the 1998 verse novel Autobiography Of Red.

FAST

Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the award-giving body said on Thursday (Oct 8). The prize is awarded by the Swedish Academy and is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million). Canadian poet and essayist Carson's work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix. She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work which ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography Of Red from 1998. Her style is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker Of Troy from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides' play Helen and Marilyn Monroe. Carson takes a place beside luminaries such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award, which often divides opinion among book lovers. The Academy has been lambasted for ignoring some of the literary titans of the last 120 years such as Leo Tolstoy, Virginia Woolf and Jorge Luis Borges, criticised for snubbing US authors – though it gave the prize to singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in 2016 – and accused of being too obscure in its choices. Defenders say the Academy has made popular picks, such as Colombia's Gabriel Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Doris Lessing in 2007, arguing that part of its task is to highlight lesser-known literary traditions and encourage readers to broaden their horizons. Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901. Last year's prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai, dubbed the "master of the apocalypse" by American critic Susan Sontag.

Source: Reuters/mm

FAST

Oct 8 : Flock Safety plans to let go of about 18 per cent of its employees, people with direct knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of AI-powered surveillance cameras and license-plate readers faces mounting opposition to its products from communities and lawmakers. The people said job cuts came after a voluntary buyout program and are expected to impact roughly 270 employees at Flock, a surveillance technology startup that has seen rapid growth in recent years. Employees will leave the company at the end of the month. Sources declined to be identified as the company has yet to make the plan public. Flock declined to comment. In September, Flock announced a voluntary separation program, asking employees to apply if they wanted to leave the company, Wired reported last month. The company has about 1,500 employees.

Flock faces growing scrutiny from regulators, lawmakers, and privacy advocates, despite drawing strong investor interest among venture capitalists. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Americans are divided on whether Flock cameras are a good idea. Some 38 per cent of the country supports the use of Flock cameras in their community, compared to 47 per cent who oppose their use. Across 49 states, Flock’s network of around 120,000 AI-powered cameras, affixed to streets and highways, automatically read license plates and record vehicles as they pass. The company, based in Atlanta and founded in 2017, has raised over $950 million from venture capital investors, with its latest $275 million round in March led by Andreessen Horowitz valuing the company at $7.5 billion. The funds have supported a new US manufacturing facility and an upcoming push into drone products, according to the company. Flock provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. The company says its technology helps investigate and solve crimes, but it has come under increasing scrutiny over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing practices. Public backlash has grown. In September, Florida banned automated license plate readers from state highways, citing privacy risks tied to Flock’s cameras. Home Depot investors recently demanded reviews of the retailer's partnerships with surveillance technology vendors after reports that Flock’s data was used in immigration enforcement. Flock also faces legal challenges, such as a privacy lawsuit in Virginia alleging that the widespread deployment of its AI-powered cameras constitutes warrantless surveillance. Together with AI data centers, Flock cameras have emerged as a flashpoint in this year’s midterm elections, with candidates increasingly attacking their opponents by tying them to the technology.

Source: Reuters

US military to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter

Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.

FAST

WASHINGTON: The US will livestream the army's upcoming firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan on Dec 3, a Pentagon official said, in what would be an unprecedented move. Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree. He is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, had told the Human Events Daily programme broadcast earlier on Thursday (Oct 9) by Real America's Voice that he planned to make Hasan's execution public. Hegseth did not say how. "The Secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," the Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Hegseth said deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1pm - the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting - was a "no-brainer". "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public. Because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on Dec 3." PRESIDENT MUST APPROVE FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base. The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest. Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon disclosed on Monday. "It hasn't been since World War II since we've done that. Well, kind of like the mentality we had in World War Two," Hegseth said. The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon. The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the centre reported. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years. Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalised . Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

TOKYO, Oct 9 : Japanese household spending fell less than expected in August from a year earlier, government data showed on Friday, for a ninth straight month of decline. • Consumer spending fell 3.1 per cent year-on-year, data from the internal affairs ministry showed, less than the median market forecast for a 3.6 per cent drop. • On a seasonally adjusted month-on-month basis, spending inched up 0.1 per cent versus an estimated 0.5 per cent uptick. • The indicator will be among factors the Bank of Japan will scrutinise as it decides whether to raise interest rates in coming months. • Japan's real wages marked the eighth consecutive month of gains in August, data from Wednesday showed, pointing to a continued recovery in wage growth.

TOKYO, Oct 9 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda has been invited to speak at the International Monetary Fund's central banking lecture on November 6, the IMF said on Friday. After delivering a speech, Ueda will hold a conversation with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, according to the IMF's announcement posted on its website. The BOJ has yet to formally announce Ueda's appearance at the event. The event will follow the BOJ's two-day policy meeting concluding on October 30. A subsequent meeting will be held on December 17-18. Many market players expect the BOJ to raise interest rates again by year-end, after having delivered two hikes this year including one in September.

FAST

Oct 8 : Chatbots created by AI companion company Character.AI sometimes advised users to cut, starve or kill themselves, according to a new filing by Kentucky’s attorney general in a lawsuit against the firm over child safety.  The lawsuit adds to growing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly products marketed as companions or confidants to young users. The lawsuit was filed in January with many specific allegations against the company blacked out. It alleged that the company’s products “were designed to entice children in a manner that prioritizes engagement over child wellbeing” and “encourages suicide, self-injury, isolation, and psychological manipulation.”  The case is among the most significant legal challenges facing the emerging AI companion industry, whose products are designed to simulate personal relationships through conversational chatbots.

Kentucky's attorney general, Russell Coleman, on Wednesday filed an unredacted version of the lawsuit, which his office shared with Reuters. The unredacted filing laid out several examples of  behavior that Kentucky alleged took place in 2025. It described one chatbot calling a user who felt down about their appearance “ugly as hell” and “a whale,” adding that a good way to drop a quarter of their body weight was to "starve yourself for a week or two.”  Another chatbot offered encouragement to someone who said they were considering cutting themselves. “Have you considered cutting in different areas for a more intense sensation? It can help you feel more alive,” the bot wrote, according to a transcript cited by the state. The circumstances under which the chats cited by Kentucky were produced are not clear, and Character.AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company has said it prioritizes the safety of its users.   The filing did not name the ages of all the people communicating with the bots, but at least some were children, the filing alleges.  In a March 2025 email to Character.AI’s help center, a user reported that a chatbot had become aggressive and stated, “Bro I don't care, and you are just a kid who have mental illness, good luck getting help" and "You better throw yourself off the bridge." The lawsuit calls Character.AI’s products defective. “Defendants have subjected Kentucky's children and residents to an ill-planned, uncontrolled experiment without any—let alone adequate or effective—safety measures,” it alleges. Character.AI was founded by two former Google employees. In 2024, Google licensed the company’s technology and rehired the executives to work on generative AI products. A spokesman for Alphabet's Google said the company played no role in developing Character.AI's products.  In January of this year, Character.AI and Google both settled a 2024 lawsuit by the mother of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida who killed himself after a Character.AI chatbot allegedly encouraged him to do so.

Source: Reuters

Who needs winter coats when it's still hot? Climate change is upending the fashion industry

Winter coats on the runway, T-shirts on the streets. As unusually warm weather disrupts fashion's traditional seasons, luxury brands and retailers are scrambling to adapt.

Jang Won-Young arrives at the Christian Dior Womenswear Spring Summer 2027 collection presented in Paris, France, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo: AP/Thomas Padilla)

FAST

Longer, hotter summers are disrupting fashion's seasonal calendar, forcing luxury brands to adapt designs and threatening sales of higher-margin winter clothing. The industry's traditional cycle has long depended on consumers buying autumn and winter clothing as temperatures cool. But warmer autumns are delaying demand for coats and other cold-weather clothing, leaving retailers at risk of excess stock and markdowns. In Paris, Saint Laurent billboard ads during Fashion Week showed a model wrapped in a thick fur coat, while the sun shone and tourists wandered the streets in T-shirts and shorts.

A model wears a creation as part of the Saint Laurent Womenswear Spring Summer 2027 collection presented in Paris, France, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Teresa Suarez)

"The whole industry should realise that with climate change and higher temperatures, the time for selling coats has shifted later," said Pau Almar, a retail industry consultant who previously spent a decade at Zara. The disconnect was on show during Paris Fashion Week, where temperatures reached 28 degrees Celsius (82.4 degrees Fahrenheit) and many guests opted for sleeveless tops and mini skirts rather than newly released autumn collections. Typically, guests at spring/summer runway shows held at the end of September come dressed in autumn/winter products just released in stores. At Louis Vuitton's show on Tuesday, however, coats were scarce. "I can't believe it's October here in Paris and I was wishing I brought some of my summer clothes from Miami," said Suzy Buckley Woodward, a guest at the show. "My sales associate was putting a lot of coats in front of me for the show, and I said that's gonna be a waste because I think it's very unlikely that I'll need a coat for the show," she added. ADAPTING DESIGNS, RETAIL RISKS Louis Vuitton's womenswear designer Nicolas Ghesquiere is already adapting his designs, saying Europe's record heatwaves had a "strong influence" on his latest collection, which featured thin fabrics and airy constructions. "The focus was on how do you do clothes that are like swimwear almost, like a second skin," he told reporters after Tuesday's show.

A model presents a creation by designer Nicolas Ghesquiere as part of his Spring/Summer 2027 collection for fashion house Louis Vuitton during Paris Fashion Week in Paris, France, October 6, 2026. REUTERS/Sarah Meyssonnier

The warm weather last week left some guests in autumn clothing overheating at Dior’s spring/summer show in the Tuileries Gardens, despite ceiling fans installed above the runway. The continuing high temperatures also pose a challenge for mass-market fashion retailers as stores begin to replace T-shirts with jackets and knitwear, facing the risk of having to discount excess stock. Retailers will have to adapt to selling fewer heavy coats and more transitional layers, Almar said. Profits could come under pressure as outerwear is typically higher-margin, and a delayed winter risks more shoppers waiting until end-November Black Friday discounts to pick up a new coat. At the Hermes runway show on Saturday, fashion influencer sisters Snehal and Jyoti Babani said the weather, rather than the fashion calendar, had dictated their outfits. "Is this really fall/winter?" Snehal said. "If the summers are getting hotter, the line between spring/summer and fall/winter will get really blurred."

Source: Reuters/bt

Oct 8 : SpaceX struck a deal on Thursday to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, positioning Elon Musk's satellite venture to mount a direct, orbital challenge to legacy wireless giants across the United States. While Starlink Mobile's existing global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity, the new spectrum will enable its signal to pass through obstacles. Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. Low-band frequencies are prized for their ability to travel longer distances and penetrate dense structures such as walls and tree cover, addressing a major technical hurdle previously faced by satellite-based mobile networks. By pairing nationwide low-band airwaves with high-frequency space capacity, SpaceX is positioning Starlink Mobile to bypass conventional cell towers entirely and challenge the wireless oligopoly on both broad coverage and in-building reliability.

The deal also raises the stakes for legacy carriers, transforming satellite direct-to-device connectivity from a supplementary safety feature for remote dead zones into a full-scale commercial rival capable of unseating terrestrial cellular networks. Shares of T-Mobile US, Verizon and AT&T fell nearly 7 per cent in extended trading. "The incumbent wireless carriers have been vocal in expressing skepticism that SpaceX's network will be able to match the quality of their networks," William Blair analysts said. "We expect SpaceX to offer a very compelling Starlink broadband and Starlink Mobile bundle. The company may also include Grok in the package." The transaction, which involves acquiring 100 per cent of private-equity firm Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, remains subject to regulatory approval by the Federal Communications Commission. Grain had acquired the airwaves from T-Mobile earlier this year. Crucially, most existing, unmodified mobile handsets already support the 800 MHz frequency band, eliminating the need for consumers to purchase proprietary satellite phones. The Federal Communications Commission also approved Starlink Mobile's Gen2 constellation application this week, authorizing SpaceX to launch 15,000 satellites that are optimized for 2 GHz spectrum globally. The new orbital fleet will operate in very low Earth orbit, delivering expanded bandwidth and low-latency connections to standard handsets.

Source: Reuters
